mcqs.question: You build the Z-array of pattern + '#' + text to search for a match. What tells you a match occurs at a given position in the text?
options: Z[i] equals the length of the pattern at that position
Z[i] equals 0 at that position
Z[i] equals the length of the text at that position
Z[i] equals the position of the separator character
mcqs.explanation: Z[i] equal to the pattern's length means the substring starting there matches the entire pattern prefix — exactly a full match. A Z-value of 0 means no match at all, and the other two options don't correspond to any meaningful signal in this construction.

mcqs.question: In the Z-array construction, what does the line z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l]) accomplish when i falls inside the current Z-box [l, r)?
options: It resets z[i] to 0 as a safe starting point
It picks a safe lower bound from already-known information — either the remaining room in the box or the mirrored match length — so only the extension past that point needs direct comparison
It directly copies z[i - l] without any adjustment
It skips computing z[i] entirely and moves to the next index
mcqs.explanation: The min of the box's remaining room and the mirrored Z-value gives a value guaranteed not to overrun what's already proven true, avoiding redundant re-comparison of characters already known to match — the character-by-character while loop then only extends past that established floor. Copying z[i-l] directly without the min would be unsafe once the match would run past the box's right edge.

mcqs.question: In the pattern + separator + text construction, why must the reported match index be adjusted by subtracting (pattern length + 1)?
options: Because the Z-array is 1-indexed rather than 0-indexed
Because Z-values are computed modulo the pattern length
Because the combined string's coordinates are offset from the text's own coordinates by the length of the pattern plus the separator character
Because the separator itself counts as two characters
mcqs.explanation: A position i in the combined string sits (pattern length + 1) characters ahead of the corresponding position in the text alone, since the pattern and separator precede it — subtracting that offset converts back to the text's own indexing. The Z-array is 0-indexed exactly like the combined string, and separators are exactly one character.

mcqs.question: Why must the separator character used to join pattern and text not appear anywhere in either string?
options: A Z-value could legitimately extend across the pattern/text boundary and produce a false or corrupted match count
The separator is only a formatting convenience and has no effect on correctness
It would make the combined string too long to process in O(n)
It would cause the Z-array construction to throw a runtime error
mcqs.explanation: If the separator appears elsewhere in the input, a match could extend past the intended boundary between pattern and text, since the algorithm has no other signal marking where one string ends and the other begins. It doesn't affect the O(n) time bound and doesn't cause a crash — it silently corrupts the answer, which is the more dangerous failure mode.

mcqs.question: Both KMP's LPS array and the Z-array run in linear time and solve substring search. What's a genuine practical difference between them?
options: KMP's LPS array is built over the pattern alone, while the Z-array is naturally built over pattern-plus-text combined, making period and border problems more directly readable off the Z-array
The Z-array cannot be used for substring search at all, only for period-finding
KMP's LPS array requires more memory than the Z-array in every case
The Z-array only works on strings shorter than the pattern
mcqs.explanation: The Z-array's setup — comparing a string against its own prefix, which naturally extends to pattern+text — makes periods and borders a direct one-line check (p + Z[p] == n), while deriving the same facts from KMP's LPS array takes an extra logical step. Memory use between the two is comparable, and both fully support substring search.

mcqs.question: For a string s of length n, which condition identifies p as a period of s using the Z-array?
options: Z[p] equals p
Z[0] equals n - p
p times Z[p] equals n
p + Z[p] equals n
mcqs.explanation: p + Z[p] == n means the match starting at position p runs all the way to the end of the string, which is exactly the condition for p being a valid period — the prefix of length p, repeated, reconstructs s. The other conditions don't correspond to the period definition at all.
